generatedProse.concept-context: In academic study, a critical edge begins as you read. You set each source against the others: linking findings, comparing methods, weighing the strength of the evidence. The hard part is carrying that engagement into your writing. Two moves do most of the work. First, use sources actively, leading with your own argument. Second, flag your criticality with the language of criticality: hedges such as 'suggests', contrast markers such as 'however', and inference markers such as 'this implies' show the reader you are weighing the evidence.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students writing about the same two sources.

{{learner-a}} writes: the first source reported a positive result, and the second source reported one too. The sentence is true and the sources are there, but nothing signals a critical mind at work. The two sources simply sit next to each other. A reader cannot tell what the writer makes of them, because no judgement has been voiced. This is reporting without a critical edge.

{{learner-b}} writes: the first source suggests a positive result; however, its evidence was thin, which implies the finding should be read with caution. The second source, by contrast, is stronger and points the same way, so the case is firmer than either alone. Here the language of criticality does visible work. The reader can see each move: a hedge, a contrast, an inference, an evaluation. This is a critical edge.

Both students read the same sources. Only {{learner-b}} made their criticality visible on the page.
generatedProse.summary: A critical edge, in any subject, starts as you read and shows in how you write. You use sources actively, leading with your own argument, and you signal your criticality with the language of criticality, so a reader can see each move. You can now tell critical writing from writing that only reports, and name the move a critical phrase signals. With structure, sources and a critical edge in place, your writing can carry a real argument.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s passage critical where {{learner-a}}'s only reported?

items.text: They hedged, contrasted and drew an inference, so the reader could see judgements being made.
They mentioned more sources than {{learner-a}} did.
They avoided taking any position on the sources.
They quoted the sources directly instead of summarising them.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} made their criticality visible through hedges, contrasts and an inference.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about visible judgement, not the number or form of the sources.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} hedged, contrasted and inferred, so judgement was visible. The others change the count, form or stance, not the criticality.
